question: Do the cited 1905 introduction and 1918 first-record claims establish the Philippine or Pasig origin of Monopterus albus, after tracing their source chain and historical taxonomic identity?

method.summary: Compared the 2021 rice-eel article statement with the source it cites, Guerrero (2014), the bibliography of the 1989 chapter, Fowler (1918) bibliographic records, the DLSU dissertation abstract, a 2017 taxonomic conference paper, the NMNH Division of Fishes catalog, and the USFWS 2025 risk-screening synthesis. Historical claims remain attributed and separate from contemporary Pasig population evidence.
accessNotes: Publisher-indexed text for the 2021 article and the online full text of Guerrero (2014) were reviewed. The 2021 article direct page returned HTTP 502; its publisher PDF result exposed the relevant article text.
The 1989 Juliano, Guerrero, and Ronquillo chapter was not retrieved; its citation and its role in the source chain were verified through bibliographic records only.
Fowler (1918) was verified bibliographically but its original Copeia pages were not retrieved or read.

The public author-uploaded text of Chavez, Arcilla, and Carandang (2017), the DLSU dissertation abstract, and the USFWS 2025 PDF text were reviewed. A public NMNH Division of Fishes catalog query found 14 Philippine lot records with prior identification Monopterus albus and current catalog name Ophisternon bengalense, USNM 135196–135209. The paper does not publish accession numbers, so exact paper-to-catalog linkage remains inferred; see the focused crosswalk review.
No access control was bypassed and no source files, specimen records, images, or tables were retained.
method.reuseFinding: No item-specific republication permission was verified for the article, dissertation, conference paper, report, or historic bibliography. Only attributed research summaries are retained.

sourceFindings.scope: The article states that Monopterus albus was introduced to the Philippines in 1905 for aquaculture and cites Juliano et al. (1989) and Guerrero (2014). Its field study concerns rice fields in Cagayan Valley.
sourceFindings.limits: The 1989 chapter was not retrieved. The article provides no Pasig or NCR specimen evidence, and the 1905 statement cannot be independently traced to an eel-specific dated record from the reviewed chain.
sourceFindings.attribution: Retain 1905 as Ame and Mayor's statement, not as a verified Philippine-wide or Pasig-specific introduction year.

sourceFindings.scope: The article title covers introduced fish in the Philippines from 1905 to 2013; its introduction says Juliano et al. reported 34 freshwater fish introductions over 1905–1988. The Monopterus albus table row lists Malaysia as origin, year as unknown, and culture/natural breeding/wild status codes.
sourceFindings.limits: The 1905–2013 and 1905–1988 ranges are periods for broad reviews, not an eel-specific date. The table does not substantiate 1905 for Monopterus.
sourceFindings.attribution: Use the table's unknown year when describing what Guerrero (2014) reports; do not transfer the review's start year to this species.

sourceFindings.scope: Bibliographic records identify the cited chapter as pp. 83–90 in Exotic Aquatic Organisms in Asia and confirm its relevance to Philippine fish introductions.
sourceFindings.limits: The chapter text was not obtained. It is unknown whether it gives a species-specific 1905 date, a broader national introduction period, or any specimen/source detail for Monopterus.
sourceFindings.attribution: Keep the chapter as an unresolved source-chain lead; do not claim it confirms the 1905 eel date.

sourceFindings.scope: Bibliographic records identify Fowler's A List of Philippine Fishes in Copeia 58 (1918), pp. 62–65. Later works cite this list as an early Philippine Monopterus albus inventory.
sourceFindings.limits: The original pages were not reviewed. A publication or inventory year is not necessarily the date an animal arrived, and the cited bibliographic record contains no Pasig locality or specimen identifier.
sourceFindings.attribution: Describe 1918 only as the year of a cited historical inventory unless original specimen and collection metadata are located.

sourceFindings.scope: The dissertation abstract says the eel was introduced and first recorded in the Philippines in 1918; it reports opportunistic samples from four Luzon sites.
sourceFindings.limits: The abstract does not name the four sites. The full dissertation was not reviewed, and its summary does not establish the identity or status of a Pasig population.
sourceFindings.attribution: Retain the 1918 wording as the dissertation abstract's claim, distinct from an independently verified introduction date.

sourceFindings.scope: The 2017 paper's abstract says the first inventory was in 1917, while its main text describes Fowler's 1918 inventory. It reports that 14 Philippine lots once catalogued as Monopterus albus were reclassified as Ophisternon bengalensis, based on a personal communication with Smithsonian curator David Smith; the authors say they examined sample Smithsonian specimens in 2016.
sourceFindings.limits: The paper prints no catalog or accession identifiers, locality-by-lot table, determination dates, or direct Smithsonian link for those 14 lots. The 1917/1918 discrepancy remains unexplained. A separate NMNH search returns exactly 14 Philippine Specimen/Lot entries with prior identification Monopterus albus and current catalog name Ophisternon bengalense; the count and name crosswalk strongly corroborate the report, but the paper does not explicitly identify USNM 135196–135209 as its set.
sourceFindings.attribution: Treat the 14-lot count and taxonomic reclassification as strongly corroborated by the museum catalog while keeping exact paper-to-catalog-set linkage inferred. It cautions against treating the historical name as confirmed modern Monopterus.

sourceFindings.scope: The public NMNH Division of Fishes catalog has 14 Philippine Specimen/Lot records, USNM 135196–135209, each with current catalog name Ophisternon bengalense and prior identification Monopterus albus. The records are dated March–August 1908 and list Manila Market or Malabon Market locality wording; all list the Albatross Philippine Expedition, 1907–1910, and raw NMNH field acqln=065731 (field label not interpreted).
sourceFindings.limits: The catalog market labels are not capture-site evidence and do not identify a river, lake, or other source water. NMNH states that only slightly over half of its holdings are online and geographic retrieval fields may be inaccurate. No direct Fowler specimen or Commercial Museum transfer link is present in the reviewed records.
sourceFindings.attribution: This is primary catalog support for a 14-lot historical name crosswalk. The agreement with the 2017 paper is strong but the paper omits the accession numbers, so their exact correspondence is not explicit. It establishes neither introduction timing nor present-day occurrence, habitat, native status, or invasiveness.

sourceFindings.scope: The 2025 synthesis describes Monopterus albus as a likely species complex, reproduces the IUCN Philippines native-range classification, and separately summarizes swamp eels brought from Malaysia for aquaculture. It says those later introductions have unknown dates and counts but are presumed after about 2000; it also attributes a 2008 Nagadacan rivers introduction account to northern Luzon residents.
sourceFindings.limits: These are attributed secondary accounts and do not resolve the historical Fowler specimen, identify which taxon-complex members were moved, or establish any Pasig occurrence or origin.
sourceFindings.attribution: Keep the later aquaculture/community accounts distinct from the 1905 and 1918 claims and do not generalize them to NCR.

sourceChainAssessment.1905Claim: Reported by Ame and Mayor (2021), which cites Juliano et al. (1989) and Guerrero (2014). The directly reviewed Guerrero table records the Monopterus year as unknown, and the 1989 chapter remains unread. Thus the cited source chain does not verify the species-specific year 1905.
sourceChainAssessment.1917Or1918Claim: Fowler's 1918 publication is cited as an early Philippine inventory; the 2017 paper has an internal 1917/1918 discrepancy, and Nisperos (2022) calls 1918 the first country record. NMNH catalog dates place the 14 market-labeled lots in 1908, before Fowler's publication, but do not identify their source waters or prove a species introduction date. None of these dates identifies a modern Pasig eel.
sourceChainAssessment.historicalIdentity: The 2017 paper's report of 14 Philippine Monopterus-labelled lots reclassified to Ophisternon bengalensis is strongly corroborated by 14 public NMNH records, USNM 135196–135209, whose prior identification is Monopterus albus and current catalog name is Ophisternon bengalense. Because the paper prints no accession numbers, identifying those records as the exact reported set remains a strong count/name inference rather than an explicit cross-reference. The catalog localities are Manila/Malabon market labels and cannot be treated as capture waters or as Fowler's specimen. The USFWS synthesis further notes that M. albus as historically used encompasses a probable complex.
sourceChainAssessment.laterIntroductionAccounts: The USFWS summary describes later Malaysian aquaculture introductions, presumed after about 2000, plus a locally attributed 2008 Nagadacan account. These may concern different populations or taxa and do not adjudicate the Pasig record.
sourceChainAssessment.resolution: The dates are not a simple contradiction: 1905 is framed as an introduction date, while 1918 is framed as a first inventory/record date. However, the 1905 date is not verified in its cited source chain; the 1918 historic name is taxonomically contested; and later introductions are also reported. The origin and identity of the Pasig fish remain unresolved.
sourceChainAssessment.decision: Do not label the Pasig fish native, introduced, invasive, or confirmed as Monopterus albus from this source chain. Do not add an occurrence row or public species projection.

scopeAndReuseDecision.decision: Research-only historical source-chain review. No public species assertion, occurrence row, image, diet, geometry, catchability, rule, or app projection.
scopeAndReuseDecision.paperToCatalogSetLinkage: strong count-and-name agreement; exact accession linkage inferred, not explicit

nonClaims: The review does not establish that the first eel introduction to the Philippines occurred in 1905, 1918, or after 2000.
No claim is made that all Philippine or Pasig swamp eels are native or introduced.

USNM 135196–135209 strongly match the 2017 paper's reported 14-lot count and prior/current names, but the paper does not print their catalog numbers; exact identity with the authors' set is not explicit.
The Manila and Malabon market locality labels do not establish the original capture water or habitat of the 14 catalog lots.
No historical specimen from Fowler is linked to Pasig, NCR, or a named waterbody.
Four unnamed Luzon dissertation sampling sites are not assigned to NCR or Pasig.
No present-day presence, abundance, season, fishing legality, safety, diet, or bait recommendation is made.
nextActions: Obtain and read Juliano, Guerrero, and Ronquillo (1989), pp. 83–90, to determine whether it provides an eel-specific date and its underlying citation.
Retrieve Fowler (1918) and any associated Philadelphia Commercial Museum/Smithsonian accession data; compare dates, locality labels, original determinations, and current determinations.
Retrieve and read Fowler (1918), then seek an explicit Commercial Museum-to-Smithsonian or Fowler-to-USNM cross-reference before linking any of the 1908 market lots to Fowler's specimen.
Seek the Pasig fish assessment table, specimen vouchers, station localities, collection dates, and any diagnostic or genetic methods before resolving its taxon or population origin.
Continue NCR freshwater, brackish, and marine evidence discovery; this review does not change regional baseline or completion status.
